 Seoul sees China’s unofficial Hallyu ban easing, but K-Pop concerts are another matter Seoul sees China’s unofficial Hallyu ban easing, but K-Pop concerts are another matter
 A breakthrough FTA expansion into services opens the door for South Korean film co-productions, but screening hurdles remain, and the deal does not guarantee the return of K-pop concerts to China.
 Ji Da-gyum
 The Korea Herald
View all posts by Ji Da-gyum → 
 People watch the arrival of US President Donald Trump at the entrance of a subway station near his hotel during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong province on November 18, 2026. PHOTO: AFP
 November 20, 2026
 SHENZHEN – South Korea has made progress toward easing China’s unofficial restrictions on Korean entertainment following a breakthrough in bilateral free trade negotiations on services and investment, including cultural content and tourism, according to Cheong Wa Dae.
 But the deal does not guarantee the return of K-pop concerts to China.
 “Rather than meaning that concerts by Korean singers can now be held freely, it means more channels have opened up for us to continue seeking approval for such performances through discussions with China,” a senior presidential official said during a briefing Wednesday on condition of anonymity.
 The remarks came after South Korea and China declared the substantial conclusion of follow-up negotiations on services and investment under their bilateral free trade agreement, following a summit between President Lee Jae Myung and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday.
 The agreement is expected to ease barriers facing South Korean businesses in China across industries including film, gaming, tourism, retail, construction, legal services and finance, while strengthening investment protections and regulatory transparency.
 The breakthrough has raised expectations of an easing of China’s “Hallyu ban,” a set of unofficial restrictions that have hindered South Korea’s entertainment industry in the Chinese market for nearly a decade.
 The restrictions emerged in 2016 after Seoul decided to deploy a US Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, missile defense system, drawing strong objections from Beijing.
 Although China has never formally acknowledged imposing a ban, South Korean entertainers have faced barriers to staging concerts, appearing on Chinese television and distributing films and other cultural content in the country.
 “The Hallyu ban cannot really be regarded as an official measure by China,” the official said. “But there are certainly aspects that we perceive that way.”
 The official said the conclusion of negotiations on services and investment under the FTA marked progress in addressing those restrictions by securing “most-favored-nation treatment” for South Korean cultural content.
 “The agreement confirmed that Korean content would not be treated less favorably than content from other countries,” the official said. “In that sense, we can say there has been some progress in addressing what we perceive as the Hallyu ban.”
 Why K-pop concerts remain a question mark 
 Concerts, however, remain a separate matter.
 “China has certain sensitivities when it comes to concerts,” the official said. “The agreement does not contain a provision requiring either country to approve performances by singers from the other country.”
 The official suggested that China’s cautious approach stems partly from the nature of live performances, which can draw large groups of fans.
 “Much of this content is consumed individually at home. But concerts bring fans together in one place,” the official said. “China appears to have a different approach to this kind of fan culture, and its authorities may view large-scale concerts differently than we do.”
 Despite the absence of an explicit commitment on concert approvals, the official said Seoul had gained more room to engage Beijing on the issue.
 “Even so, we believe more channels have opened up for discussions,” the official said. “We think we can explore various options, starting with those that China would find less burdensome.”
 While acknowledging that Beijing’s treatment of concerts could be seen as a shortcoming, the official said the agreement represented “significant progress overall in expanding the presence of Korean culture in China.”
 The agreement marks a breakthrough after years of negotiations stalled partly over China’s reluctance to open its cultural market. The two countries began follow-up negotiations on services and investment in 2018, following the entry into force of their original FTA in 2015.
 “In previous negotiations, China had insisted on excluding the cultural sector from the talks,” the official said. “That led to a prolonged suspension of formal negotiations.”
 Negotiations resumed around 2025, though difficulties persisted. The official pointed to a series of meetings between Lee and Xi, particularly their January summit, as a turning point in the talks.
 “After the South Korea-China summit in January, China began presenting a somewhat improved position on key areas of interest to us, including culture and tourism,” the official said. “That helped accelerate the negotiations.”
 Can Korean films break through? Hurdles remain 
 The agreement could also open new opportunities for Korean films in China, particularly through joint productions.
 The senior official said films co-produced by South Korea and China could qualify for treatment under China’s domestic film quota system, offering a potential route into Chinese theaters.
 “If we make a film together, it could be screened in China under its domestic film quota system,” the official said.
 Cheong Wa Dae earlier announced that Lee and Xi had agreed to pursue cooperation on joint film productions during their summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday.
 But questions remain over whether the agreement will lead to more Korean films reaching Chinese theaters, given that only one Korean film has received a theatrical release in China over the past decade.
 Another government official, also speaking to reporters on condition of anonymity, noted that films must pass China’s content review process before they can be released in theaters, a hurdle that remains for Korean films despite the breakthrough in bilateral FTA negotiations on services and investment.
 “Now that we have secured a commitment to most-favored-nation treatment, if this situation continues, we would be able to raise questions about whether Korean films are effectively being discriminated against,” the official said. “We also believe we would be able to represent the interests of Korean companies through consultations with China.”
